summary:
Kerala maintains a state-level transgender policy and welfare architecture that predates and runs alongside the national framework. In November 2015 it adopted India's first government transgender policy, providing for identification as male, female or TG (third gender), equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, and non-discrimination on grounds of sex. Kerala was reported to Parliament in December 2021 as one of the states and union territories that had constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules.

Transition-related care is nominally subsidised but unevenly available. In March 2016 the Social Justice Department proposed free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, at least in medical colleges, from the following financial year; the state later provided reimbursement for gender-affirming surgeries. Training gaps mean many government hospitals cannot perform the procedures, pushing patients toward costlier private institutions, and reimbursement requires patients to raise funds before they are refunded. The Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam opened a clinic exclusively for transgender patients in 2017, operating twice a month with a specialist panel and also serving sex workers, after a District Legal Services Authority proposal prompted by reports that transgender people feared approaching hospitals and relied on self-medication; the same authority proposed separate public toilets for transgender people to the district collector. The Government Medical College Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram completed its first sex reassignment surgery in January 2017. The suicide of Anannyah Kumari Alex after alleging a botched gender-affirmation procedure prompted protests and led the state to appoint an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and to begin steps toward free surgeries in government hospitals.

Kottayam's clinic issues health cards denoting transgender status, a documentation practice a visitor should expect to encounter at state facilities. Welfare measures include scholarships for transgender students in classes 7 to 10, a Kannur district budget allocation for employment and skill training, and a 2017 Social Justice Department workshop in Kozhikode with around 30 transgender representatives covering identity cards, pensions for those over 60, skill development, scholarships, educational loans and driving lessons for employment as Uber drivers. A transgender-owned and operated G Taxi service was launched to provide livelihood and public visibility. A transgender school opened in Kochi in 2016 to prepare students for 10th and 12th board examinations and vocational training for ten students aged 25 to 50; it ceased operating as a school after three months and became a hostel for transgender Kochi Metro staff. A Gender Park opened in Kozhikode in February 2016.

Policing is the sharpest risk area. Reports describe a spate of killings of transgender people with inadequate police investigation, and a rise in police harassment when transgender people approach stations to file complaints, which produced a Director General of Police direction that grievances be received without delay. In October 2023 the annual pride march in Malappuram was attacked by a mob and police carried out a lathicharge. In December 2023 the High Court of Kerala described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a serious issue and directed authorities to act. The suicide of Praveen Nath, described by Minister R. Bindu as a martyr, drew attention to transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism, with the minister attributing it to cyberbullying and media transphobia.

Recorded cases under the Transgender Persons Act are few nationally and concentrated in a small number of states. Kerala accounted for 2 of the 7 national cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023, joint-highest with Tamil Nadu. These are raw counts against very small national totals, and the reporting itself attributes the low figures to bias in police registration rather than to low incidence; they are not a per-capita measure of risk and do not establish that Kerala is more dangerous than a less populous state.

Community infrastructure is comparatively developed. Queerala campaigns on sensitisation of healthcare, curricula and workplace policy; Queerythm runs a 24-hour helpline for members in distress; Sahayathrika serves female-born LGBTIQA+ members. Kerala Queer Pride has been held since July 2010 in Thrissur, and Queerythm has run annual walks since 2017 focused on sensitising police and media. An estimated 25,000 transgender people live in the state, around 81 per cent of whom wish to transition and 76 per cent of whom conceal their identity for fear of non-acceptance; societal discrimination in employment and housing and implementation gaps in state schemes remain documented problems.
tangentialFactors:
Kerala's early policy lead and its delivery record diverge. The 2015 policy and the welfare board exist on paper, but the sources describe surgeries unavailable in most government hospitals, reimbursement that requires upfront payment, and a transgender school that closed within months. A visitor relying on state-subsidised transition care should expect private-sector costs and delay.

The state's identification categories (male, female, TG) were set in 2015, before the national recognition framework was amended in 2026. State welfare schemes keyed to the TG category therefore operate on a different classification from the one now governing national legal recognition.

Kerala's recorded case count under the Transgender Persons Act is joint-highest with Tamil Nadu, but both sit inside national totals of 7 and 11 cases, which the reporting attributes to police-registration bias. The comparison carries no implication about relative safety between the two states.

Facilities provision is unresolved rather than settled: separate public toilets for transgender people were proposed by a District Legal Services Authority to a district collector, and no adoption is recorded in the sources.

outOfScopeNotes:
The 2016 proposal for free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals was pending health ministry approval and training of multidisciplinary urology, endocrinology, sexology and psychology teams; whether it has been fully implemented is not established by the sources.

Separate public toilets for transgender people appear only as a District Legal Services Authority proposal to a district collector. No adopted facility rule is sourced.

Beyond the appointment of an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues after the Anannyah Kumari Alex case, no state-level clinical protocol for gender-affirmation surgery in private hospitals is documented here.

Kerala-specific per-capita data on violence against transgender people was not located. The recorded case figures are raw counts subject to police-registration bias and cannot be converted into a rate.
